articles.title: Mastering Incident Correlation in Microsoft Defender XDR
articles.excerpt: In modern Security Operations Centers (SOCs), the sheer volume of telemetry can lead to alert fatigue, where critical security signals are lost in the noise. How the Engine Decides What Belongs Togeth…
articles.body: In modern Security Operations Centers (SOCs), the sheer volume of telemetry can lead to alert fatigue, where critical security signals are lost in the noise. Microsoft Defender XDR is designed to combat this by transforming isolated alerts into cohesive, actionable incidents. It ships with advanced features that provide a full set of customizations, allowing you to control how you handle alerts and how the system correlates them based on shared entities, artifacts, and attack behaviors. How the Engine Decides What Belongs Together At its core, the Defender correlation engine is designed to minimize manual triage. When alerts hit your environment, the system doesn’t just log them; it analyzes them for relationships.
articles.author: Boula Akladyous

articles.title: When Pay-Per-GB Proxy Pricing Stops Making Sense
articles.excerpt: High-volume data collection creates a simple but expensive pricing problem: when a crawler transfers more data, a pay-per-GB bill rises at exactly the same time. That model can be perfectly reasonable…
articles.body: High-volume data collection creates a simple but expensive pricing problem: when a crawler transfers more data, a pay-per-GB bill rises at exactly the same time. That model can be perfectly reasonable for small or irregular workloads. It becomes harder to forecast when collection runs continuously, retries increase, or several workers operate in parallel. The two pricing models 1. Pay per GB The cost is directly tied to transferred traffic: traffic cost = transferred GB × price per GB This is easy to understand and often economical for short tests. The drawback is that every retry, duplicate response, large asset, and failed extraction still consumes metered traffic. 2. Throughput-based, unmetered access A throughput-based plan uses a fixed speed and a fixed duration.
articles.author: Michael Guy

articles.title: VS Code remembers the commands you hid with a space
articles.excerpt: VS Code's Run Recent Command list, in a new window on my laptop. Note the space before export. The token's a fake. The top four were typed on a different machine. I'd opened a Debian server with Remot…
articles.body: VS Code's Run Recent Command list, in a new window on my laptop. Note the space before export . The token's a fake. The top four were typed on a different machine. I'd opened a Debian server with Remote-SSH and put a space in front of the export, so the server's bash would skip it, and it did. The server's ~/.bash_history has cd /var/log , ls -lh and uptime , and no token. My laptop has it, and it's offering to run it again. The space trick If you've ever pasted a token into a terminal, someone's probably told you to stick a space in front. bash won't save a line that starts with one when HISTCONTROL has ignorespace or ignoreboth in it, which Debian and Ubuntu set up for you, and zsh does the same with setopt HIST_IGNORE_SPACE .

articles.title: I built an open-source ad server for AI chat apps that keeps the chat on your server
articles.excerpt: Every message in a free AI app costs the person running it money. Most users will never pay for a subscription, so ads are the obvious way to cover the bill. ChatGPT started showing ads on its free ti…
articles.body: Every message in a free AI app costs the person running it money. Most users will never pay for a subscription, so ads are the obvious way to cover the bill. ChatGPT started showing ads on its free tier this year. If you run your own AI app and want ads today, the options are not great: Join an AI ad network. It works, but the network usually needs to see the user's conversation to pick an ad, and it keeps a cut of the revenue. Build your own ad system. Matching, budgets, click tracking, fraud checks, reporting. That is weeks of work next to your actual product. Hardcode a sponsor banner. Same ad for everyone, whatever they asked. It performs badly. So I built Aside , an open-source ad server for AI chat apps that you run on your own server, next to your app.

articles.title: Let Claude Code or Cursor debug your page in a real Chrome browser

articles.body: When Claude Code or Cursor fixes a front-end bug, it is usually guessing. It reads your source, but it cannot see the page, the console errors or the network calls. The Chrome DevTools MCP server closes that gap: it lets your coding agent control and inspect a live Chrome browser, so it can reproduce a bug, read the real error and check that its fix worked. Here is the setup, using the commands from the README. The short version is on the Deduped use-case page . What it gives your agent chrome-devtools-mcp is a Model Context Protocol server that exposes Chrome DevTools to an AI coding assistant such as Claude, Cursor, Copilot or Antigravity. According to the README it does three main things: Performance insights : records traces with Chrome DevTools and extracts actionable findings.

articles.body: It came from outer space, exploding high above the South Atlantic off the coast of Argentina. That April 1 event — an incoming meteor , also termed a bolide — was observed by both U.S. space-based military and civil sensors. Hush-hush U.S. government satellite sensors detected the speedy fireball cutting through our atmosphere. The object's brightness peaked at an altitude of nearly 60 miles (90.5 kilometers) over the South Atlantic. That dazzling spectacle was also caught by the National Atmospheric and Oceanic Administration's GOES-E and Europe's Meteosat Third Generation (MTG) Imager-1 satellite. Those two independent spacecraft in geostationary orbit detected the bolide via onboard lightning imagers.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 1, 1962: The Soviet Union Launches Mars 1 spacecraft to Red Planet during the Space Race
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 1, 1962, the Soviet Union launched the Mars 1 spacecraft on a mission to fly by the Red Planet. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 1, 1962, the Soviet Union launched the Mars 1 spacecraft on a mission to fly by the Red Planet. While it did end up flying by Mars , the mission was not exactly a success. After it separated from the rocket, it deployed its solar panels and started cruising toward Mars. When mission controllers were checking out the telemetry it transmitted back to Earth, they found out that Mars 1 had sprung a leak in one of the gas valves that controls the spacecraft's orientation. And without a working orientation system, Mars 1 would have a hard time pointing its antennas in the right direction. It lost contact with Earth when it was about halfway to Mars . A model of Mars 1, a Mars flyby spacecraft launched to the Red Planet by the Soviet Union on Nov. 1, 1962.

articles.title: Anthropic VS code extension on Cursor backdoored for nearly 12 hours
articles.excerpt: It's still unknown how attackers got access to Anthropic's verified Cursor account.
articles.body: An official extension for Anthropic’s Claude model was backdoored and threatened as many as 5,000 developers' machines, multiple sources reported Friday. Anthropic so far has yet to warn customers of the incident. The compromised package was a VS Code extension available in the marketplace of Cursor, a maker of AI-assisted developer tools, the company said Friday. The malicious version, 2.1.313, subsequently affected “at most 5,000 users,” presumably when they either downloaded it or their systems automatically fetched and installed it. Anthropic pushed version 2.1.314 several hours after the previous version became available on Cursor, according to independent researcher Kevin Beaumont.
